imageAlt: Photograph of 1918 One Dollar Banknote with Washington Portrait
story: Your story begins with an old dollar bill. Look closely—George Washington’s face is right there! This bill was made in 1918, long after he lived.

apiFallback.title: 1918 One Dollar Banknote with Washington Portrait
apiFallback.description: George Washington is on this one-dollar bill from 1918. People still put his picture on money many years after he lived.

imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Camp Chest
story: Imagine the army getting ready to move. Washington brings this camp chest along. Inside are things he needs for cooking and eating on the journey.

apiFallback.title: George Washington's Camp Chest
apiFallback.description: Washington carried this box when he traveled with his army. It held things he needed to cook and eat.

story: Washington gets dressed in his blue and tan army coat. People can spot their leader by the clothes he wears. Can you find both colors?

apiFallback.title: George Washington's Uniform
apiFallback.description: Washington wore a blue and tan coat as an army leader. His clothes helped people recognize him.

story: Something shiny rests on Washington’s shoulders. These gold pieces are called epaulettes. Artists put them in paintings of him, too.

apiFallback.title: George Washington's Epaulettes
apiFallback.description: These gold pieces decorated Washington’s shoulders. You can spot them in some paintings of him, too.

story: You turn a corner and meet a giant Washington! An artist made him look like a hero from long ago. What do you notice about the way he sits?

apiFallback.title: George Washington Statue
apiFallback.description: This large statue shows George Washington sitting like a hero from ancient times. You can see it on the museum’s second floor.

imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington's Battle Sword and Scabbard
story: Here is the steel sword Washington wore while leading his army. It traveled with him during the Revolutionary War. Look for the long metal blade.

apiFallback.title: George Washington's Battle Sword and Scabbard
apiFallback.description: Washington wore this steel sword while leading the American army during the Revolutionary War.

imageAlt: Photograph of a brass surveyor’s compass attributed to David Rittenhouse and associated with George Washington
story: Before he led an army, Washington worked as a surveyor. Surveyors measure land to make maps. This compass is part of his map-making story.

apiFallback.title: Washington’s Surveyor’s Compass
apiFallback.description: A surveyor uses a compass to measure and map land. This one is linked to Washington, who worked as a surveyor when he was young.

imageAlt: Photograph of George Washington’s Camp Stool
story: It is time for a rest at camp. Washington can unfold this small stool and sit down. Then it folds up again for the next trip.

apiFallback.title: George Washington’s Camp Stool
apiFallback.description: Washington used this folding stool during the Revolutionary War. It was easy to carry from camp to camp.

imageAlt: Photograph of Washington’s Buff Wool Waistcoat
story: Washington gets dressed for the day. Under his army coat he wears this wool waistcoat, a kind of vest. His outfit has more than one layer!

apiFallback.title: Washington’s Buff Wool Waistcoat
apiFallback.description: This waistcoat is a kind of vest. Washington wore it under his coat during the Revolutionary War.

imageAlt: Photograph of Washington’s Buff Wool Breeches
story: Washington’s outfit needs pants, too. These wool breeches stop near the knees. Clothes looked a little different long ago.

apiFallback.title: Washington’s Buff Wool Breeches
apiFallback.description: Breeches are pants that stop near the knees. This wool pair belonged to Washington.

imageAlt: Photograph of Tenino 25-Cent Scrip with Washington Portrait
story: Many years after Washington lived, the town of Tenino needed money. It made its own paper money and put his face on it. Where else have you seen that face?

apiFallback.title: Tenino 25-Cent Scrip with Washington Portrait
apiFallback.description: When regular money was hard to get, the town of Tenino made its own paper money. Washington’s picture is on this piece.

story: The army Washington led needed long guns called muskets. He wanted these guns marked to show they belonged to the new United States. Why might an army mark its things?

apiFallback.title: US-Stamped Charleville Musket
apiFallback.description: A musket is a long gun. Washington wanted these army guns marked to show they belonged to the United States.

imageAlt: Photograph of Benjamin Lincoln’s Yorktown Sword
story: At Yorktown, the British army gave up. Washington asked another army leader, Benjamin Lincoln, to meet them. Lincoln carried this sword.

apiFallback.title: Benjamin Lincoln’s Yorktown Sword
apiFallback.description: This sword belonged to Benjamin Lincoln. Washington asked him to accept the British army’s surrender at Yorktown.

imageAlt: Photograph of Washington and Lafayette’s Scissor Glasses
story: Open, close! These glasses have handles that move like scissors. They are linked to Washington and his friend Lafayette.

apiFallback.title: Washington and Lafayette’s Scissor Glasses
apiFallback.description: These folding glasses are linked to Washington and his friend Lafayette. The two handles open like scissors.

imageAlt: Photograph of Braddock Pistol Used by Washington
story: A British general gave Washington this pistol. Washington carried it on later army trips. Now the museum keeps it safe so we can learn its story.

apiFallback.title: Braddock Pistol Used by Washington
apiFallback.description: A British general gave Washington this pistol. Washington carried it during later army trips.

imageAlt: Photograph of “Long Live the President GW” Button
story: A big day arrives: Washington becomes the first U.S. president. People celebrate by wearing little brass buttons like this one. Can you see the letters GW?

apiFallback.title: “Long Live the President GW” Button
apiFallback.description: People wore this brass button to celebrate when Washington became the first U.S. president.

imageAlt: Photograph of Washington Inaugural Starburst Button
story: People want to celebrate Washington becoming president. Here is another button they wore, with a bright star design. Can you spot its shape?

apiFallback.title: Washington Inaugural Starburst Button
apiFallback.description: This star-shaped button celebrated Washington becoming president in 1789.

imageAlt: Photograph of Bache Silhouette of George Washington
story: An artist cuts Washington’s side view from a piece of paper. The dark shape is called a silhouette. Does it look like a shadow to you?

apiFallback.title: Bache Silhouette of George Washington
apiFallback.description: A silhouette is a picture made from a person’s outline. This one shows Washington from the side.

imageAlt: Photograph of Piece of Washington’s Mahogany Coffin
story: After Washington died, people saved this tiny piece of wood from an older coffin made for him. They kept it to remember him. Even a small object can hold a big story.

apiFallback.title: Piece of Washington’s Mahogany Coffin
apiFallback.description: This small piece of wood came from an earlier coffin made for Washington. People kept it to remember him.
